final_narration:
As bodies age, some cells stop dividing but refuse to die. Scientists call them senescent cells, and they build up in tissues and seem to make ageing worse. So what happens if you clear them out?
A randomised study in mice tested exactly that. Ninety-six mice, half male and half female, all twenty-four months old, roughly the equivalent of old age. Each was randomly assigned to get a two-drug combination called D plus Q, dasatinib and quercetin, or a dummy treatment. Dosing was three days in a row, every two weeks, for sixteen weeks. The researchers scoring the results did not know which mice got what.
In fat tissue, the burden of senescent cells fell by forty-one percent compared with untreated mice. On a rotating-rod balance test, treated mice stayed on twenty-two percent longer. And they lived longer: from the start of treatment, the typical remaining lifespan rose from about twenty-one weeks to almost twenty-seven.
But not everything improved. Grip strength was no better than in untreated mice. Only fat tissue was examined, in one inbred mouse strain, at one age.
And the big caveat: this was mice. No people were involved, and this schedule and dose have never been tested in humans, so they do not translate into a human dose. It is a promising lead about how ageing might be slowed, not a treatment you can act on.
